title: Meet Jude Terry, the Next Teenage Star Ready for His USMNT Debut
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Zach Lowy11:11 AM EST18-year-old Jude Terry is already making his presence felt in MLS. / Soobum Im/MLS/Getty ImagesIt has been one year since U.S. Soccer suffered a heartbreaking round of 32 exit in the FIFA U-17 World Cup. The boys drew first blood as Cavan Sullivan latched onto Mathis Albert’s pass and dialed in a cross to Jude Terry, who made no mistake with the finish. The Baby Nats led for 70 minutes and appeared headed for the next round, only for Morocco to equalize on the cusp of stoppage time. Morocco prevailed 4–3 on penalties in Doha, bringing the Americans’ journey to a sudden and gut-wrenching conclusion.

Fast forward to today, and three members of that U-17 squad have already ascended to the senior national team. Sullivan, Albert and Julian Hall have all featured in the last two USMNT international windows, with the trio becoming cap-tied during this month’s Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti. Sullivan is now the youngest goal scorer in USMNT history, while Hall has also made history as just the second player to score five goals in his first six USMNT caps (Eddie Johnson).

Several other members of that U-17 squad, including Nimfasha Berchimas and Máximo Carrizo, could soon follow in their footsteps, but perhaps nobody is better positioned to make the jump than Terry. At just 18 years old, the midfielder is already making his mark at Los Angeles FC, and he could be poised to enter the senior national team picture come 2027.

Terry starred at the U-17 World Cup. / Jurij Kodrun/FIFA/Getty ImagesBorn and raised in Chula Vista, Calif., Terry grew accustomed to crossing into Mexico to play five-a-side and seven-a-side tournaments. It was across the border that he sharpened his technical skills against older, physically imposing opponents and developed the competitive edge that has epitomized his game.

A technically gifted midfielder with an eye for the spectacular, Terry excels at wriggling out of tight spaces, turning away from pressure and unlocking defenses with incisive passes. He has sought to model his game on two of La Liga’s finest midfielders: Pedri and Jude Bellingham, while still carving out his own identity.

“I think my technical ability is something that I’ve always taken pride in; my ability to turn and create is something that you’ve seen this year,” Terry tells Sports Illustrated. “[In terms of players I look up to], I would say Pedri; he plays really nice, or Jude Bellingham. The way they keep the ball, the ball retention, and the way they can turn on the ball and create for their team.”

“I’m just looking at their ability to beat guys by turning, by their awareness of where they are on the pitch,” Terry adds. “The way they play and the way that they make the game look so easy is something that I try to implement. That’s who I’ve been watching right now, but you always try to be your own player, try to make your own mark, so I try to focus on myself.”
THE OPENER FOR THE @USYNT 🇺🇸JUDE TERRY FINDS THE BACK OF THE NET FIRST 🔥 pic.twitter.com/y1Ft6i5Eza

Terry’s potential was crystal clear long before he made his professional debut. As a youngster, he won a tournament at Barcelona’s renowned La Masia academy, receiving the trophy from club legend Gerard Piqué himself. He also triumphed in a Manchester City skills competition, earning the opportunity to train at the club’s facilities and meet first-team stars like Sergio Agüero.

Terry joined the MLS academy in 2021, but with San Diego FC still years away from entering the league, he headed north along Interstate 5 in 2021, swapping Legends FC for LAFC. He steadily climbed through the youth ranks before signing a homegrown contract in December 2024.
By 2025, Terry earned international recognition after being named to The Guardian’s Next Generation list, which highlighted 60 of the world’s most promising players born in 2008.

Soccer runs deep in the Terry family. His grandfather played in Argentina’s second division, while his father competed in Mexico’s indoor leagues. Eligible to represent both nations, Terry initially attracted interest from El Tri but opted to represent the Stars and Stripes. He captained the Americans to their first-ever Concacaf Under-15 Championship title in the Dominican Republic in 2023 before featuring at the 2025 U-17 World Cup in Qatar.
17-YEAR-OLD JUDE TERRY WITH A BANGER FOR @LAFC 💯💯💯 pic.twitter.com/w6Xb2JPLYQ

This year, Terry has transformed from a highly touted academy prospect into a genuine first-team contender. He made his senior debut on Feb. 24, entering at halftime in a 1–0 victory against Honduran side Real España in the Concacaf Champions Cup. Three weeks later, he made his MLS debut with a late cameo in a 2–0 win against St. Louis CITY.

Terry would have to wait another month for his first start, but his patience proved to be a virtue. Handed a place in midfield by Marc Dos Santos, the teenager repaid his manager’s faith with a sensational long-range strike that brought LAFC level against the Portland Timbers at BMO Stadium. Unfortunately for the hosts, Kevin Kelsy had the final say, snatching a last-second winner for Portland.

“Obviously, when you hit the ball like that, you always hope for it to go into the top corner,” Terry told R.Org about that first finish. “To be honest, I just hit it, and after that, I kind of blanked. It was a beautiful goal, and it was a great way to start my journey in MLS.”

It was a glimpse of the audacity and technical finesse that have made Terry one of LAFC’s most intriguing young talents. Across 17 first-team appearances in all competitions, he has demonstrated his ability to dictate possession, carve open defenses and threaten opponents with thunderous strikes from distance. His performances have also earned him a place in MLS’s 22 Under 22 rankings, where he finished 20th.

More importantly, his swift ascent has provided a blueprint for the next generation of LAFC academy prospects hoping to follow in his footsteps. Having spent years climbing through the club’s youth ranks, Terry understands just how much it means to make the leap from academy soccer to the senior team, and he's keen to set an example for the next crop of youngsters.
